native component FlatString

import String.{maxLeafSize, concatAndBalanceIfNecessary, CatString, spaces}
import Stream.{...}

export FlatString


private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

lineSeparator: String = LineSeparator()

private natLineSeparator(): String = builtinPrimitive(
            "com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.lineSeparator")

private LineSeparator(): String =do
    ignore(FlatString); (* This initializes the constructor for FlatString
                   before its type is used (in the next line). *)
    natLineSeparator()
  end

object FlatString extends { String, DelegatedIndexed⟦Char, ZZ32⟧ }
    getter size() : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")
    getter asExprString() : String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.asExprString")
    getter asFlatString(): String = self
    getter asString(): String = self
    getter asDebugString(): String = asDebugStringIndented(0)
    getter depth():ZZ32 = 0

    (* With the help of trait DelegatedIndex, this defines our generate method *)
    getter generator() : Generator⟦Char⟧ =
        self.indices.map⟦Char⟧(fn (i:ZZ32):Char ⇒ self.get(i))

    getter isBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isAlmostBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isExtremelyUnbalanced():Boolean = false

    balanced():String = self

    opr |self| : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")

    uncheckedSubstring(r1: Range⟦ZZ32⟧) : String = do
    (* We could build a subString node here, but not until everything is working,
        because that will introduce
       SubString objects into code that may still expect FlatStrings.
       As written, this method always answers a FlatString.
       In any case, the FlatString object supports substring without copying*)
        assert((r1 ∩ self.bounds).isEmpty, r1.isEmpty,
                    "Empty substring of non-empty string")
        if r1.isEmpty then ""
        else self.javaSubstr(r1.left.get, r1.right.get + 1)    (* Java substr's endIndex is one past the last character *)
        end
    end

    opr =(self, other: FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.stringEquals")
    opr <(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) < 0
    opr <=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≤ 0
    opr >(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) > 0
    opr >=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≥ 0
    opr CMP(self, other: FlatString): TotalComparison =  self.cmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CMP(self, other:String):TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CMP self)
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:FlatString): TotalComparison =
      self.cicmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:String): TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP self)

    (** get skips bounds checking. **)
    get(i:ZZ32): Char =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.charAt")
    cmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareTo")
    cicmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareToIgnoreCase")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaSubstr")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32): String = javaSubstr(lo, self.size)
    javaIndexOf(c:Char): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.indexOf")
    flatConcat(self, b:FlatString):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeConcatenate")
    flatConcat(self, b:Char):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeConcatenateChar")
    javaRegExpMatches(m:FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpMatches")
    javaRegExpSplit(m:FlatString, i:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpSplit")

    indexOf(c:Char): Maybe⟦ZZ32⟧ = do
        i = javaIndexOf(c)
        if i = -1 then Nothing⟦ZZ32⟧ else Just⟦ZZ32⟧(i) end
      end

    verify():() = do
        assert(self.depth, 0, self)
    end

    asDebugStringIndented(indent: ZZ32): String =
        spaces(indent) || "J" |self| "/" self.depth ":" self

    opr ∈(c:Char, self): Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ≠ -1

    rangeContains(r: Range⟦ZZ32⟧, c: Char):Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ∈ self.bounds[r]

    (** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts to string and
        concatenates **)
    opr ||(self, b:FlatString): String = do
        if b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
             (* Since both self and b have depth 0, balancing can't be necessary *)
            CatString(self, b)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end
      end

    opr ||(self, b:String):String = do
        if self.isEmpty then b
        elif b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
        else
            typecase b.asFlatString of
                f:FlatString ⇒ flatConcat(self, f)
                f:String ⇒ concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
            end
        end
    end

    opr ||(self, b:Char): String =
        if |self| ≥ maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b.asString)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end

    splitWithOffsets():ZeroIndexed⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧ = Nothing⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧
    split():Generator⟦String⟧ = Nothing⟦String⟧

    writeOn(stream: WriteStream): () = stream.write(self)

end FlatString

end

1	# Keeping the record
2	
3	How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.
4	
5	**history**
6	: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.
7	
8	**pointer**
9	: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."
10	
11	**pass**
12	: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.
13	
14	## What an entry is
15	
16	An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
17	
18	- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
19	- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
20	- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
21	- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
22	- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
23	- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
24	- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
25	- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
26	- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
27	- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
28	- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
29	- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
30	- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
31	- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
32	- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.
33	
34	Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:
35	
36	1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
37	2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
38	3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
39	4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
40	5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
41	6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.
42	
43	In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:
44	
45	- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
46	- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
47	- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
48	- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
49	- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
50	- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.
51	
52	An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:
53	
54	- keep: every check passes;
55	- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
56	- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
57	- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.
58	
59	Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.
60	
61	## Reading and writing
62	
63	- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
64	- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
65	- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
66	- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
67	- Commit the record file and its history together.
68	- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
69	- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.
70	
71	## The pass
72

23	## 1. The question, and a primer
24	
25	**The question.** Under the static numerals, by which rule of the language or which text of the library does `u = 0` answer `true`, and `u =/= 0` answer `false`, for a number `u` equal to the numeral, on both paths, before and after the switch-over?
26	
27	### 1.1 Why the question exists at all
28	
29	A numeral has no value of its own when a program runs (P-174). Before the program runs, it becomes a value of some number type. Which type depends on where it stands (P-173):
30	
31	    u: NN32 = 0      (* the place fixes NN32: the numeral becomes the NN32 zero *)
32	    x = 0            (* nothing fixes a type: the numeral takes its default, the ZZ32 zero *)
33	    a: Any = 0       (* Any fixes no type either: the ZZ32 zero *)
34	
35	The number types are siblings. An `NN32` zero and a `ZZ32` zero are two different values, and `SEQV` says so: `false`.
36	
37	In `u = 0`, the numeral stands as an argument of the operator `=`. The one library declares many `=`. Two of them matter here:
38	
39	    opr =(a: Any, b: Any): Boolean = a SEQV b       (* the fallback, FortressLibrary.fss:96 *)
40	    opr =(self, b: NN32): Boolean = ...             (* NN32's own, FortressBuiltin.fss:449 *)
41	
42	- For the fallback, the second parameter is `Any`. `Any` fixes no type, so the numeral takes its default and arrives as a `ZZ32`. The fallback then compares an `NN32` with a `ZZ32`: `false`.
43	- For `NN32`'s own `=`, the second parameter is `NN32`. That fixes a type, so the numeral arrives as the `NN32` zero: `true`.
44	
45	Both declarations can take the call. The tree's rule picks the fallback, because the numeral reaches it without a coercion, and "a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits" (P-46; P-49 for the checker's order). So the tree answers `false`, and your design answers `true`.
46

50	    u < 0        (* NN32's < : the same *)

52	    x = 0        (* for x: RR64: the pair =(RR64, ZZ32) fits the default as it is *)

110	## 3. How the library avoids the question elsewhere, and why `=` is different
111	
112	**`u + 0`, `u < 0`.** The one library declares `+` and `<` only as methods of self-typed traits: `opr +(self, other: T): T` in `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:361`), `opr <(self, other: T)` in `StandardPartialOrder[\T\]` (`:230`), and each number type's own. No `+` or `<` takes `Any`. So no declaration fits `(NN32, numeral at its default)` as it is, the coercion attempt runs, and the numeral converts to `NN32`. Nothing special is done for numerals: the absence of a catch-all does the work.
113	
114	**`=`.** `Equality[\T\]` declares `opr =(self, other:T): Boolean = self SEQV other` in the same self-typed form (`:100-102`), and `StandardPartialOrder` extends it (`:222-223`, `:232`). But beside them stands the catch-all, the fallback over `(Any, Any)` (`:96`), and `=/=` exists only as a catch-all, `opr =/=(a:Any, b:Any):Boolean = NOT (a=b)` (`:98`), except on `QQ`, `RR32` and `Float`. A numeral at its default fits a catch-all as it is. That is the whole difference.
115	
116	**Why the library declares `=` over `Any`, with its history.**
117	
118	- 2007-01-04, the first import of the interpreter's library (`72ae6881b1`, git author `jm143038`): `opr =(a:Any, b:Any):Boolean = false` and `opr =/=(a:Any, b:Any):Boolean = NOT (a=b)` (`ProjectFortress/FortressLibrary.fss:64-65` there). The fallback meant: two values with no `=` of their own are unequal.
119	- 2008-03-04 (`d56a402b41`, git author `jmaessen`, "Preliminary (unsatisfactory) implementation of SEQUIV"): the body became `a SEQUIV b`. Two days later (`21946c933f`) the operator was respelled `SEQV`.
120	- The compiler's prelude, the team's later library, never had it: it declares `===` for a few types (`64e5f04dbf`, 2010-05-05, git author `dr2chase`, "Added definition of === for popular types") and `=` only on its types.
121	- The revival kept the fallback and gave it its meaning in P-168: "Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is strict equivalence". P-165 and F-324 lean on it: two numbers that no coercion joins compare by the fallback and answer `false` without an error.
122	
123	What the fallback is for: generic code. A `List[\E\]` compares its elements by `=` with `E` unbounded; `assert(x, y, msg)` and `=/=` compare any two values (F-280); a value object without its own `=` is still comparable. Section 6, way A, measures how much of the library stands on it.
124	
125	## 4. The team's sources
126	
127	**The Working Draft on numerals** (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-148`). A numeral has a numeral type (`:83-129`). "Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types because, as in common mathematical usage, we expect them to be polymorphic" (`:132-134`). "This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`:142-144`), and the libraries "define coercions from numerals to integers ... and rational numbers" (`:146-148`). The Draft says nothing of a numeral compared with a number. It has no default.
128	
129	**The Draft on which declaration a call takes** (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:450-456`, "Coercion Resolution"): "we first determine whether there exists a declaration that is applicable without coercion. If so, the most specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are explicitly added". This is the rule that P-46 and P-49 keep.
130	
131	**The Draft on `=`.** It declares no `=` over `Any`. `Any` has only `===` (`basic-lib/objects.tex:22-24`). `=` is a method of a self-typed trait, `opr =(self, other: T)` in `IdentityEquality[\T\]`, with the property that it agrees with strict equivalence (`advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex:134-139`), and each number type lists its own, as `opr =(self, other: ZZ)` (`basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:144`) and `opr =(self, other: QQ)` (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:133`). The operators chapter says only: "The expression `e =/= e'` is semantically equivalent to the expression `NOT (e = e')`" (`basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:262-263`), and that `<`, `<=`, `>=`, `>` "are supported by integer, rational, and floating-point types" (`:271-273`), with no word on a numeral operand.
132	
133	**Put together.** In the Draft's own language, `u = 0` has no declaration that applies without coercion, because nothing takes `Any`. So the coercion is added, the numeral becomes an `NN32`, and the answer is `true`. The Draft reaches your result through the shape of its library, not through a rule about numerals. The interpreter's catch-all is what breaks it, and the catch-all is the interpreter's own, from 2007, not the Draft's.
134	
135	**The revived specification** records today's state as a departure, not as the rule: "the interpreter answers `u = 0` false ... and whether `u = 0` is true is open" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5278-5290`; `:3813-3825` for `=/=`). Its literals chapter already says that "the parameter types of the declaration that a call invokes" are places that fix a type (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:202-204`). Its coercion chapter says the opposite for the choice: "a numeral is applicable without coercion to a parameter of its default type and to a parameter of a type that fixes no type for it; its conversion into any other type is a coercion" (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:111-114`). The revival wrote both.
136	
137	## 5. The peers, as context only
138	
139	- **Haskell, Rust, Swift.** A literal is polymorphic; `==` takes two operands of one type, so `u == 0` types the literal at `u`'s type. The default (`Integer`, `i32`, `Int`) applies only when nothing constrains the literal. None has an `==` over a top type. This is the Draft's shape (way A).
140	- **C#.** A constant expression converts implicitly to the other operand's type when its value fits, so `u == 0` compares two `uint`. A rule for constants at operators (way C).
141	- **Go.** An untyped constant takes the other operand's type in a binary operation, and its default type only where none is given. Go shows the `Any` case exactly: for `var a interface{} = uint32(0)`, `a == 0` is `false`, because the constant becomes an `int`. Every way below keeps that answer for `a: Any`.
142	- **Julia.** No polymorphic literals; `UInt32(0) == 0` is `true` because `==` on numbers compares values across types (way F).
143	- **Scala 2, Java.** `==` over the top type, with special cases for boxed numbers. Scala 3 added a restriction on `==` across unrelated types (`CanEqual`), a move toward way A.
144

155	### Way A. The Draft's shape: no `=` over `Any`
156	
157	- **Changes.** The library: strike the fallback `=` and `=/=`; each type that is compared gets its `=` from `Equality[\T\]`, and `Equality` gains `opr =/=(self, other:T): Boolean = NOT (self = other)`. Generic code that compares takes a bound, as `E extends Equality[\E\]`. No checker or walk change: `u = 0` then behaves as `u + 0` does. The specification: the library chapters, and Appendix I for P-168's fallback.
158	- **Sees.** `u = 0`, `0 = u`, `h = 0.5`, `y = 7`: `true`. `u =/= 0`: `false`. `a = 0` for `a: Any`: a static error, no declaration. Two values of types that no coercion joins, as a `ZZ64` and an `RR64`: a static error, where today the answer is `false`.
159	- **Keeps.** P-46, P-49, P-173, P-174, P-59. It is the Draft's library and the prelude's.

161	- **Cost.** Measured on a scratch copy of the library with only the fallback `=` struck: the checker reports 19 type errors in 13 places of the `FortressLibrary` component alone, such as `Could not check call to operator =`, and that count is a floor, since the checker stops a block at its first failing statement (row 474). The other library components, the tests and every generic program come on top. Several rungs, and a redesign of the library's generic comparisons.

163	### Way B. A numeral goes to the most specific declaration that takes it; the default is the last resort

291	## For the curator
292	
293	**The question, in one line.** By which means should `u = 0` answer `true`, for a number `u` equal to the numeral, now that no `=` ties a numeral type to a number type?
294	
295	**Why it is not automatic.** The library has a catch-all `=`, declared for any two values, which compares by strict equivalence. A numeral fits it at its default type, `ZZ32`. An `NN32` zero and a `ZZ32` zero are not strictly equivalent. The catch-all runs before `NN32`'s own `=`, because your rule P-46 says that a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits.
296	
297	**What I measured.** After the switch-over the compiled checker picks the catch-all too. So without a decision both paths will answer `false`.
298	
299	**The options.**
300	
301	1. Way A. Delete the catch-all `=`. This is the Working Draft's library. Then only `NN32`'s own `=` exists, and the numeral converts to reach it. It bends P-168, your decision that every value is comparable by `=`. It is the largest: at least 19 errors in the library's main component alone.
302	2. Way B. Change the rule for numerals only. A numeral goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own conversion if need be. The default is the last resort. It bends P-46 and P-49, for numerals only. One rung.
303	3. Way C. A rule for operators: the other operand fixes the numeral's type. It bends P-173, P-46 and P-49, and it needs exceptions, as for `x^2`. One to two rungs.
304	4. Way D. Bring the `=` pairs back, in a static form. It is against your word that the pairs were a wrong choice. A program's own number type would have to declare them too.
305	5. Way E. Make the catch-all generic, `opr =[\T\](a: T, b: T)`. Promotion, the rule by which a generic call runs at the narrowest type that both arguments convert to, then fixes the numeral. It bends one sentence of P-165: two number types that share a conversion target would compare by value. It needs two repairs of promotion first. One rung.
306	6. Way F. Let every number type compare by value with the default types. It gives a wrong answer for `q = 0.1` with a rational `q`. Not carried further.
307	
308	**What every option leaves alone.** `a = 0` for a value `a` typed `Any` stays `false`. microGPT's lines do not change.
309	
310	**My recommendation.** Option 2, way B, built in the checker and in walk in one rung, before the switch-over. It is the rule that your design's own sentence states, it keeps the pairs deleted and the catch-all in place, and its bend of P-46 and P-49 is limited to numerals. 1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22

The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. 70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
117	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
118	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
119	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
42	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
43	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
44	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
45	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
46	
47	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
48	
49	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
50	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
51	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

content.content:
- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. His own broader rule is not taken: to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration, and to fall back to a plain one only when none does. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. P-49 gives the order in which the checker tries a call. Row 537: the compiled dispatch between two generic declarations of one name with different bounds.

- P-49 **The compiled checker tries a call first by subtyping, without the expected type, and coerces its arguments only when that attempt is not kept.** The expected type is the type that the call's context requires. The checker's first attempt checks the call by subtyping alone, without the expected type. It keeps that attempt when its result converts to the expected type, by coercion if need be. If it does not keep that attempt, it tries coercion of the arguments, with the expected type. So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one that coercion reaches. Why: in the curator's words, coercion should be tried when there are no matches.

- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174); `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types, whose names and static parameters are the Draft's (P-174), and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's, which it leaves out. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3, but for the numeral types' form, which P-174 holds. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.

- P-174 **A numeral's type exists only at compile time: the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, below `Numeral`, with its four numbers as static parameters; every number type, the library's too, takes a numeral through a coercion generic over the four numbers.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r` and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`), so `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`; the four are naturals of any size, and read as values in a coercion's body they are exact integers, `ZZ`; this implementation's `NN32` bound (P-40) is for sizes. The coercion's body calls the type's constructor on values computed from the four numbers, as in `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Interval(roundDown(v, r, m), roundUp(v, r, m))`, and the compiler instantiates it for the numeral and folds it (P-176). No numeral value exists when a program runs: a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type, and is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. A numeral has no sign: at a program's type `-3` is the type's own prefix `-` applied to the coercion's result for `3`, and a type without `-` refuses it; any other expression of numerals alone folds first (P-173) and reaches such a type only through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`, since coercions do not chain. The design leaves out the binary chapter's numeral coercion and `opr ||` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1662`). Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations", and has libraries define the coercions into integers and rationals (`literals.tex:132-148`); the curator finishes that design, in place of the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). Rows 960 and 981 hold where the tree departs: the digit count of `00.5`, and walk running a numeral type written in a `comprises` clause.

- P-176 **A numeral at a place denotes one value, the same on both paths and made once: the compiler folds the coercion instantiated for it (P-174), and walk runs that coercion at the place's first evaluation.** Where the result is a JVM `int`, `long`, `float` or `double`, the class file holds it as a constant; otherwise, as at `QQ` or a program's own type, the constructor call on the constants runs once per place, into a `static final` field filled when the class loads, and a program's type's own `-` on the numeral (P-174) runs there too. Walk fixes the coercion's static arguments from the numeral's four numbers and keeps the result for the place; it refuses a numeral only when the place runs, until it runs the checker (P-12). Before the switch-over the compiler's prelude carries this design (P-37), so that both paths give one value at one place. Why: a numeral is a constant of the program, and a JVM class file holds no object, so a field filled once at load is the nearest form of an object constant. Row 957 holds where the tree departs: a place whose type names a type parameter.

- P-76 **An integer numeral has the Working Draft's type `NaturalNumeral` (P-174), which each of the eight number types converts from: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32`.** Where nothing fixes a type it is a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit (P-173). `NaturalNumeral` takes the place of `IntLiteral`, the name that the compiler's prelude and the interpreter's library gave the type, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic goes, since an expression of numerals alone folds before the checker (P-173). Walk, before it runs the checker (P-12), converts an integer numeral from its exact value at each place that fixes a type, and elsewhere evaluates it at its default, which walk already gives it by its value (F-74). Walk gaps: coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511).

- P-58 **Every native binding is a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper.** A native binding is a library body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, the library's own form, and it keeps that form. Why: the language has no foreign-function interface, only a planned one, so the library's own practice decides the binding's form. Its string is to name a static Java method in `nativeHelpers/`, the compiled path's helpers, such as `"com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intLT"`, in place of a glue class of walk, which the compiled path cannot use (F-32). Walk is to load the named helper through a loader beside its glue classes. For the runtime's own operations walk's loader answers the helper's name with walk's own operation instead: `ilkName` and `SEQV` (P-167), and the 13 bindings of the arrays' store, threads with `abort` and the task trace (P-169). At the parse, before the checker, the compiled path is to rewrite each such body into a synthetic `import java` of the helper and a call, and to refuse a string that names no helper. The bindings move onto helpers step by step, and from the step that moves a binding, the compiled checker checks it against the helper's Java signature, not all at once at the switch-over. The other form, `import java` declarations written in the library itself, is not taken. F-32 counts the bindings that still name a glue class.

- P-168 **What `SEQV` means, on both paths: the specification's rule, with no special case for any type.** Values of different types are never strictly equivalent; two value objects of one type are when their fields are, tuples element by element and floats by their bit patterns; two reference objects are only when they are one object (`Specification/basic/objects.tex`, "Object Equivalence" and "Value Objects"). Both paths read the `value` modifier. Each path changes its own code: walk drops its equivalence across types (row 909) and its answer `true` for value objects whose body declares no field (row 113); the compiled helper `equality.sEquiv` gains the rule for value objects, tuples and floats (rows 906 and 907; the prelude's own `===` keeps row 908 until the switch-over). `ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects (P-166). Strings are reference objects: the library declares `FlatString`, `CatString` and `SubString` without `value`, so two such strings are strictly equivalent only when they are one object, and text equality is the strings' own `=`; P-171 makes two literals of one text one object. This overrules the team's code on both paths, walk's `seqv` and the prelude's `opr ===(a:String, b:String) = a=b`, where the specification is silent on strings. A program with a `value object CC64` tests it on both paths beside the review's 14 cases (F-326). Why: the specification's rule read as written, over the team's unfinished code of 2008 and 2010, which its authors called preliminary and incomplete; P-167 makes this one comparison that both paths answer. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4; `reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md`, sections 3 and 7.

- P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until it runs the checker, after the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type. The specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. The curator accepts this as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. After the switch-over, once walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12 orders the two steps), it uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.

- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'

**The team's sources.**

Jan-Willem Maessen, a co-author of the specification who owned the library and its parallelism (`research/authorship.md`), made the primitive array in 2007 (`9645d6c05`, 2007-08-31, "Created a primitive vector type", by `git log --follow`). 2. `PrimImmutableRR64Array` is Maessen's unboxed store, a `double[]` (`interpreter/glue/prim/PrimImmutableRR64Array.java:39-46`). He added it in `353818213`, 2008-07-28: "When you request an immutable array of RR64 these should be used in preference to the boxed version." No factory chose it then or chooses it now: `git grep` finds it only in `NativeArray.fss`.
3. The team's later word: the prelude has no generic array (row 305). Christine Flood, who built the transactional memory and the compilation to fork/join (`research/authorship.md`), wrote the 2011 vectors (`f4973a717`, 2011-08-16, "Simple Integer 1 dimensional arrays"). They hold a Java array inside a run-time class: `FZZ32Vector` over an `int[]`, `FStringVector` over a `String[]` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FStringVector.java:14-19`). Their helpers take the class (`nativeHelpers/simpleIntVector.java`, `simpleStringVector.java`). The table reads the class as the prelude's trait (`NamingCzar.java:337-340`), and the class implements that trait (`FStringVector.java:15`). This is P-164's device. It is also how the team met F-106's limit: the helper takes the wrapper, never the Java array.
4. Compiled code sends each read and write of a mutable cell through the transaction inside `atomic` (`fortress-repo` skill, `references/compiler.md`, "The runtime"; `compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). A compiled store must do the same for its elements. Walk's `AtomicArray` does this for walk.
5. A helper's Java signature has no type parameter. Its element is an `Object`, which the checker reads as `Any` (`NamingCzar.java:451`, `:487`). So a read at `T` goes through the library's `cast` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:33-37`), a `typecase`, by P-162's pair with a private bare half at `Any`. The other way is a checker rule for a binding at a type parameter.

**What the compiled path needs before any `double[]` store exists.** Five bindings: `PrimitiveArray`'s `get`, `put` and `init00`, and `PrimImmutableArray`'s `get` and `init00`. Every array, vector, matrix, varargs list and `ArrayList` reaches them (section 1, finding 1). `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s two are reached by nothing.

**The peers.** JVM languages store a generic array of references in an `Object[]` and cast at the read (Java's `ArrayList`, Scala's `ArrayBuffer`). They keep a primitive array unboxed: Scala's `Array[Double]` is a `double[]`. That second half is decision A's ground (P-84, P-85).

**The ways.**

- **(a) Wait for decision A, after the switch-over** (PLAN:60). The compiled path then cannot run any array of the one library at the switch-over (finding 1). As an order, this does not work.
- **(b) A boxed store now, behind P-164's device and P-167's device.** The one library declares a trait for a Java store, with walk's native object below it, a table entry, and a run-time class that implements it. A helper class takes a Java class that holds an `Object[]`, as Flood's vectors do, and its writes go through the compiled transaction (point 4). `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` become plain objects over a field of that trait. Walk's half is P-167's device, so walk keeps `AtomicArray` and its values. Decision A later gives `RR64` its `double[]` in the same frame. Touches: `NativeArray.fss` and `.fsi`, `FortressLibrary` (the trait), the walk-world table (`NamingCzar.java:464-504`), a helper class, a run-time class, P-167's table, and a native constructor in walk. One rung, as large as W, the batch's largest: 0.5M for its worker (B27:315), and more with the four-thread atomic runs (`references/compiler.md`, "Testing an edit here").
- **(c) (b) with walk calling the helper through an `Object` carrier.** This is the Any-carrier review's option (a): four lines in the loader and two in `compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java`, measured (`reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 6 (a), points 2 and 3). It keeps P-58's walk half. But walk's arrays then leave `AtomicArray`, so walk's writes inside `atomic` lose their transaction, unless the helper store is also made transactional for walk's tasks.
- **(d) A code-generator intrinsic.** The class loader gives a `PrimitiveArray` instance its own array field. This is decision A's way A4, which F-18 calls unmeasured (P-84). The strings would stay glue, against P-58's form. It is decision A's work, not preparation for it.
- **`PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s two** fit (b): a compiled class over a `double[]`, as `FZZ32Vector` holds an `int[]`. No factory chooses it until decision A answers P-85's first question.

its own:

`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,

# Record writer's report: his two decisions of 2026-11-10

Both decisions are in POSITIONS, PLAN and the review queue, committed and pushed. All three checks pass. No FACTS entry changed.

One thing was unprompted by the brief: this record writer ran at 2026-11-13 23:13 UTC by the container's clock, so the new PLAN-history heading is dated 2026-11-13, while the decisions stay dated 2026-11-10.

## Entries changed or added

Old texts are whole in `POSITIONS-history.md` (blocks stamped 2026-11-13), each with his messages and their times. Below, "unchanged" means the rest of the entry stands word for word.

### P-46 (rewritten)

**Title, old:** "A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits."
**Title, new:** "A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, except a numeral's own conversion."

**Old sentence replaced:** "His own broader rule is not taken: to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration, and to fall back to a plain one only when none does."

**New text in its place**, sentence by sentence, with what each rests on:

1. "The exception is a numeral at a call."
   - Rests on: 11:33, "I think one is fine", option one being way B.
2. "A comparison of a number with a numeral answers by the number's value, and the programmer does not retype the numeral: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, and no way that answers `false` is accepted."
   - Rests on: 11:29, "of course this needs to answer true. We should not have to retype the 0 as NN32 just because the ZZ is our default", and "If any of these options causes us not to answer true for such a comparison, that is out of the question."
3. "Of the ways to `true` that the review of them offers, the curator took its way B, whose rule is in the review's words, not his: a numeral is applicable to a parameter that fixes no type, at its default, and to a parameter whose type declares a coercion from the numeral's type, by that coercion (P-173); among the applicable declarations the most specific runs, and where two are not ordered, the one that the default fits."
   - Rests on: 11:33, "I think one is fine and I don't think I have categorically excluded it before."
   - The rule is the review's section 6, "Way B", "The rule", and is marked in the entry as not his wording.
4. "So `NN32`'s own `=` runs, and not the library's `=` over `(Any, Any)`, which the numeral fits at its default `ZZ32` and which answers `false` by `SEQV` (P-168)."
   - Rests on: the review's sections 1.1 and 6 (way B, "Sees"). It is a consequence, not his words.
5. "A value typed `Any` or `Number` fixes no type for the numeral beside it, which keeps its default."
   - Rests on: P-173 as it already stood, and the review's 6.0. His "if possible" (11:29) is the nearest word of his; he did not say this.
6. "His own broader rule, to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration and to fall back to a plain one only when none does, so holds for a numeral's own conversion; for a value's coercion it is not taken."
   - Rests on: his broader rule of 2026-09-28 in P-46's history; the coordinator's statement to him that option one follows it for numerals; 11:43, "I'm happy. ... Maybe I was misquoted and we are all in alignment already."

**Added at the end**, after the row 537 sentence: "Rows 973 and 966: walk answers `false` for `u = 0`, and `true` for `u =/= 0`, which follows `=`. Detail: `reviews/numeral-equality-ways-2026-11-10.md`, "Way B. A numeral goes to the most specific declaration that takes it; the default is the last resort"."
- Rests on: F-346 and the two rows. This describes the tree, not his words.

### P-49 (one sentence added)

Added after "So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one that coercion reaches.":

"A call with a numeral argument is the exception: where the numeral's own coercion reaches a more specific declaration than the first attempt chose, that declaration runs, so `u = 0` for `u: NN32` is checked at `NN32`'s own `=`, with the numeral an `NN32` (P-46 gives the numeral's rule and its ground)."

- Rests on: 11:29 and 11:33 as above, through way B's "Bends" line ("P-49's order, for a call with a numeral: the first attempt is no longer kept as it stands").
- He did not word the checker's order. The sentence states what way B requires, not the review's mechanism of comparing two attempts.

### P-173 (one sentence added)

Added after "`gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49).":

"The parameter types of the declaration that a call runs are places that fix a type, and a numeral argument goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own conversion if need be, with its default as the last resort: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, the numeral an `NN32` at `NN32`'s own `=` (P-46 gives the rule and its ground; rows 973 and 966 hold where walk departs)."

- Rests on: 11:29, "we need to infer that the type in this comparison is between equal types if possible"; 11:33, "one is fine".
- The middle clause is the coordinator's summary of option one, as the brief gives it.
- The first clause is the revived literals chapter's, as the review quotes it (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:202-204`). I did not open the chapter.
- The `gg(5, w)` sentence stays true under way B, by the review's section 6.

### P-58 (one sentence added)

Added before "F-32 counts the bindings that still name a glue class.":

"One exception: the 28 bindings of the library's `Reflect` component keep naming walk's glue classes, for walk only, since reflection has no compiled analogue (F-32); so `Reflect` and the components built on it run under walk alone (P-177, QuickCheck's place on the compiled path)."

- Rests on: 14:03, "This sounds good to me. Why should I say one? Well, one.", to part (1) of the recommendation.
- "since reflection has no compiled analogue" is F-32's fact, not a reason that he gave. The history says so.

### P-177 (new, in "The suites and the gate")

No entry owned QuickCheck: P-160, P-161 and F-324 only mention it. Full text:

"**QuickCheck is a testing tool that the project goes on relying on: it is to run on the compiled path after the switch-over, by its static choice of generators.** `QuickCheck` (`Library/QuickCheck.fss`) picks the generator for a property's static type, and imports no reflection. `ReflectiveQuickCheck` builds on it for generic properties: it picks random types for a property's static parameters through `Reflect`, whose 28 native bindings stay on walk's glue, for walk only (P-58, the exception for `Reflect`). So the reflective component runs under walk alone, and what the team's test of it covers is to stay covered on the compiled path too: the nine generic properties of `ProjectFortress/tests/ReflectiveQuickCheckTest.fss` are checked at written types on both paths. Why: the curator calls QuickCheck an important testing tool. Detail: `reviews/quickcheck-widen.md`, sections 1 and 2."

- **Title and "Why":** 13:58, "I would say QuickCheck is important. Testing tool, and we should continue relying on it."; 14:03, "QuickCheck goes to the compiled path after the switch-over with its static generator choice. Yeah, that makes sense."
- **Sentences 2 and 3** are facts that I read: `Library/QuickCheck.fss:9-13` imports no `Reflect`; `Library/ReflectiveQuickCheck.fss:10` imports it; `reviews/quickcheck-widen.md`, sections 1 and 2.
- **"is to stay covered ... checked at written types on both paths":** part (2) of option one, which he took with "Well, one". His own sentence on coverage at 14:03 was a question ("Will the part ... be rewritten so that whatever it covers stays covered and works also on the compiled path?").
- The "new test" is not in the entry. It is in PLAN, as the coordinator's default.

## Sentences of the brief that his words did not bear out

- **"what the reflective test covers is to stay covered on the compiled path too", given as his decision.** His words there are a question. I wrote it into P-177 on the ground that part (2) of the option he took says it. If you read his "one" more narrowly, that clause of P-177 is the one to cut.
- **Part (1), the exception for the 28 bindings.** It rests only on his assent to the recommendation as a whole. He gave no words or reason of his own for it.
- **"option one was the review's way B".** This holds for the coordinator's three options. The review's own list for him numbers way A as option 1 and way B as option 2. The queue's line for item 487 said "way 1 of" the review, which a reader would take as way A; it now names way B and notes the review's numbering.
- **The two quotations to check in P-46's history.** Both are there, word for word: "C-O. Both recommendations for batch N accepted." (block of 2026-10-22 08:30Z) and his broader rule (block of 2026-10-13 18:16Z).

## Where the record already said otherwise, or stays as it is

- **P-174**, "no `=` with a number type": stays true. Way B keeps the pairs deleted; the numeral converts before `=` runs.
- **F-346 and F-341**: stay true. They state what walk does, with rows 973 and 966 open.
- **F-32**: unchanged. Its sentence on `Reflect`'s 28 is true, and P-58 now carries the exception.
- **P-59** says that walk is not changed for its choice of coercion before the switch-over. Way B changes walk's dispatch, or waits for P-12 (the review's way B, "Cost"). He did not decide that timing and I did not touch P-59; it is a question for the rung's brief.
- **The `fortress-repo` skill** ("Fortress as a language", the bullet on numbers) still says without exception "A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits." I did not edit the skill.
- **Queue item 487 was already in the answered list** before this work, filed by climb batch 30's landing. I corrected its line and did not move it.
- **PLAN line 12 and queue item 487** still name "climb batch 30b's equality rung", which the boot note says climb batch 31 replaces. I left that as it was.

## PLAN and queue edits

- **PLAN, "Where we stand", "Next":** the sentence that his answer "goes into POSITIONS, by a record writer" now says that it is in POSITIONS (P-46, with P-49 and P-173; item 487).
- **PLAN, phase 4, the natives line, D2:** the open question on `Reflect`'s 28 is replaced by his answer of 14:03 UTC, with P-58's exception and P-177.
- **PLAN, phase 4, new sub-line under D2**, marked "The coordinator's default, not a decision of his": with the switch-over, a new test carries the reflective test's nine generic properties at written types on both paths.
- **PLAN, phase 4, the list of his answers needed before the switch-over:** item 437 removed.
- **PLAN, phase 5, new line** before the list of his answers, marked the same way: after microGPT compiles, a review of ways for reflection on the compiled path.
- **PLAN-history:** new section "His two decisions of 2026-11-10 written into the record, 2026-11-13", with the three earlier lines word for word.
- **Queue, item 437:** head line and item block removed from "Code generation and the run time" (15 to 14); filed in "Answered by a decision of his" (98 to 99) with his words of 13:58 and 14:03. Counts: 185 to 184 open, 74 to 73 consequential, "Before the switch-over" 26 to 25.
- **Queue, item 487:** its answered line now cites P-46 with P-49 and P-173, his words of 11:29 and 11:33, and way B.
- PLAN lines 734, 744 and 751 ("his answer of 11:3x ... `u = 0` is `true`") were already in line and are unchanged.

## Checks

- `record.py check --base 003ecbfef2`: "record.py check: FACTS.md 283 entries, POSITIONS.md 103 entries; 0 failures; reported: size 2".
- Entries of mine over 600 characters, each kept for the sentences that stop a worker deciding wrong: P-46 2454, P-49 982, P-173 3534, P-58 1674, P-177 900.
- `queue-check.py --root . --base 003ecbfef2`: "queue-check: 496 items, 0 new (none); open 184, consequential 73, routine 111; pass".
- `plan-moves.py --root . --base 003ecbfef2`: "plan-moves: 3 lines taken out of PLAN.md; PLAN-history.md gained 10 lines, under 3 headings", then "plan-moves: pass; 3 PLAN lines to look at". The three LOOK lines are for information: line 12 names item 487, which is settled; the other two are not lines of mine.

## Commits

Both are pushed to `main`, `claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` and `blinded-fable`; `git log origin/main..main` is empty.

- `1c6a9db46f`: POSITIONS and its history (P-46, P-49, P-173, P-58, P-177).
- `11fce28e89`: PLAN, PLAN-history and the review queue.

I touched no other file. The apply file is scratch, at `/home/user/fortress/tmp/recwriter/apply.md` (gitignored).
